rows.etymology: 860. Bng. nĩṅgṛɔ or nigṛɔ adj. ‘(leading) downwards (e.g., path)’, perhaps also nĩṅgsɛṇɔ v.i. ‘to come out, slip out (e.g., baby at birth, piece of wood out of a bundle of wood)’ (with -s- suffix) and also with different suffixes (i.a. < OIA STHĀ ‘stand’) niũ̄ṭhɔ ‘(leading) downwards (e.g. a path)’, Sir.shim. nīṭho ‘down’, Jaun. nīṭhī ‘down’, Pāḍ. naiṇḍ ‘down’, Shor. niũdō ‘down’, Deog. nīṅgɛ ‘down(wards)’, and Jaun. nĩ̄galō ‘low’ and nĩglō ‘down’ — Paš. niṅg or neṅgy ‘to descend’ and naṅgic ‘descended’ (LSI [viii, ii: 105]), Paš.DN. niṅ- ‘climb down’ and soṛ-niṅ ‘sunset’ and Paš.deg. neṅgé̄k ‘putting off; dropping off’, Dm. nag- ‘(to) go down’, nəṅgaṛ ‘to bend down’, Gaw. naṅgi- ‘to descend’, Kamd. nˈiṅ ‘down’ and probably also in the Ning. name of the village niṅgalām literally ‘lower village’ (with lām ‘village’ < OIA grá̄ma- ‘village’ [4368]) all < OIA *nyagra- (ní-agra) ‘pointing downwards’. Jaun. nĩ̄galō and Bng. nĩṅgṛɔ have a morphologically and semantically reverse correspondence in Jaun. uglō, Ku. and N. algō all ‘high’ which derive < OIA udagra- ‘high, tall, long’ with -l- extension (see above p. 545). Note: The same prefix ní ‘down, in’ is found also in OIA nigam- (nigacchati) ‘to settle down upon or near’ or RV nyāgam- ‘to come down towards’. Sub OIA *nigāti ‘learns’ (7165) Turner quotes RV nyágāt ‘went down’, and he quotes two modern reflexes, namely Ash. niṅá̄- ‘to know, recognize’ and Wg. niṅā- ‘to understand’. To these to be added are Wg. niṅaˈla ‘wise, a sage’ (semantically corresponding with Ar.-Pers. ḥakīm), Saṇ. niṅa- ‘to realize, know’ and Garh. nīgṇū ‘to understand’ (Z.). It seems, however, that in Turner 7165 two different verbs came together, namely OIA nyāgam and OIA nigam- the latter of which also means ‘to acquire knowledge’.

rows.etymology: 860. Bng. nĩṅgṛɔ or nigṛɔ adj. ‘(leading) downwards (e.g., path)’, perhaps also nĩṅgsɛṇɔ v.i. ‘to come out, slip out (e.g., baby at birth, piece of wood out of a bundle of wood)’ (with -s- suffix) and also with different suffixes (i.a. < OIA STHĀ ‘stand’) niũ̄ṭhɔ ‘(leading) downwards (e.g. a path)’, Sir.shim. nīṭho ‘down’, Jaun. nīṭhī ‘down’, Pāḍ. naiṇḍ ‘down’, Shor. niũdō ‘down’, Deog. nīṅgɛ ‘down(wards)’, and Jaun. nĩ̄galō ‘low’ and nĩglō ‘down’ — Paš. niṅg or neṅgy ‘to descend’ and naṅgic ‘descended’ (LSI [viii, ii: 105]), Paš.DN. niṅ- ‘climb down’ and soṛ-niṅ ‘sunset’ and Paš.deg. neṅgé̄k ‘putting off; dropping off’, Dm. nag- ‘(to) go down’, nəṅgaṛ ‘to bend down’, Gaw. naṅgi- ‘to descend’, Kamd. nˈiṅ ‘down’ and probably also in the Ning. name of the village niṅgalām literally ‘lower village’ (with lām ‘village’ < OIA grá̄ma- ‘village’ [4368]) all < OIA *nyagra- (ní-agra) ‘pointing downwards’. Jaun. nĩ̄galō and Bng. nĩṅgṛɔ have a morphologically and semantically reverse correspondence in Jaun. uglō, Ku. and N. algō all ‘high’ which derive < OIA udagra- ‘high, tall, long’ with -l- extension (see above p. 545). Note: The same prefix ní ‘down, in’ is found also in OIA nigam- (nigacchati) ‘to settle down upon or near’ or RV nyāgam- ‘to come down towards’. Sub OIA *nigāti ‘learns’ (7165) Turner quotes RV nyágāt ‘went down’, and he quotes two modern reflexes, namely Ash. niṅá̄- ‘to know, recognize’ and Wg. niṅā- ‘to understand’. To these to be added are Wg. niṅaˈla ‘wise, a sage’ (semantically corresponding with Ar.-Pers. ḥakīm), Saṇ. niṅa- ‘to realize, know’ and Garh. nīgṇū ‘to understand’ (Z.). It seems, however, that in Turner 7165 two different verbs came together, namely OIA nyāgam and OIA nigam- the latter of which also means ‘to acquire knowledge’.
